articles.text: The stock-holders of the Northern Pacific will doubtless be well pleased with the report of the earnings for the last month. The passenger as well as the freight business is having a boom, bouble-headers constantly running on the passenger trains.
articles.summary: Northern Pacific stockholders should be pleased with last month's earnings; passenger and freight business booming.

articles.text: Mr. Martin's promised weather report appears in this issue and presents as remarkable an array of figures as we have ever seen published concerning the weather. Really the most remarkable point in the whole, is that there was no sickness on account of the heat; a fact attributable to our clear, dry climate. The report is the substance of much work and will well bear careful reading.
articles.summary: Note commending T. Martin's weather report printed in this issue and remarking that the heat caused no sickness.

articles.text: In brief, the instructions for the collection of the tax on oleomargarine are as follows: No extra employes are allowed for the collection. A tax of fifteen cents per pound is placed on imported oleomargarine. Unstamped or unwholesome products are to be sold for axle grease. Manufacturers are required to file a bond of not less than $5,000. The factory books are to be open to inspection the same as distillery and brewery books. Manfactures must display a sign on their factory, giving their name, business and number. Each package must have the word "oleomargarine" plainly printed on it in letters not less than one-quarter of an inch square. It is learned that nearly half the oleomargarine made in the United States is exported and that a large share of this comes back in the shape of fancy cheeses.
articles.summary: Summary of the federal instructions for collecting the new tax on oleomargarine.

articles.text: The Bismarck Tribune of Tuesday has a full table by counties of the Territorial assessment. It has been found that the assessors very generally undervalued property and in some of the counties this will make considerable difference in their rates of taxation. The average levy on the territory at large this year is only two and four-tenths mills; a reduction of from twenty to forty per cent. over anything hitherto levied. Billings county just hits the average, our levy being two and four-tenths mills. Interest at the rate of five-tenths of a mill brings our levy to two and nine-tenths mills. The average valuations for the Territory are: Lands, per acre; $3.87; horses, per head, $51.01; mules, $58.40; cattle, $15.63; sheep, $1.27; swine, $2.24. The rates are based on these figures; any county ranging below getting a higher rate and vice versa. Billings county's valuation was: Horses, $26; mules, $25; cattle, $16., making a very fair average for the whole.
articles.summary: Bismarck Tribune's territorial assessment table: Billings county levy 2.4 mills (2.9 with interest) and its valuations of stock.

articles.text: Either the undertaker who furnished the coffin ordered for George Fraser seized the opportunity to turn it into an advertisement or the Bismarck Tribune is guilty of letting a desire for sensationalism run away with its sense of decency. The day after George was killed, the Tribune contained an article to the effect that Sheriff Willard had had a fight with a couple of cow-boys, that he had killed them both and that it was for one of them that the coffin had been ordered. There was not a word of truth in the article and it was so mixed up with an advertisement of a fine line of furniture that it looks as though the man who furnished the coffin is at the bottom of the affair. The people of Medora and the Bad Lands are heartily sick of these lies which are scattered broad-cast about us, generally with no foundation whatever. Especially in the case of George Fraser is such an article looked upon with indignation. We think we are correct in stating that he never had a dispute here of any kind. He was a sober, industrious young man, always had a pleasant word for everyone and was a universal favorite.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy denounces a false Bismarck Tribune story, tied to a furniture advertisement, about the killing of George Fraser, whom it calls a sober, well-liked young man.

articles.text: The cowmen of the Bad Lands, like those of some of the older ranges, are brought face to face with the fact that there are about as many cattle on the range as it will support in safety. There is room for those already here and their increase, but there will be this year nearly if not quite 40,000 additional head brought in. This increase cannot be repeated with safety to the ranges. There is no disguising the fact that even this year the capacity of the ranges may be tested severely. If there are any extensive prairie fires, there is sure to be a crowding of ranges and consequent loss. Already there is some talk of taking measures, as other districts are doing, to protect the ranges from over-crowding. This can be done in a measure by convincing new-comers that there is no room for more cattle, but it would hardly be consistent when the old outfits are bringing in cattle by thousands. It would be good policy for all to rest on their oars until next spring at least, and by that time the capacity of the ranges will be well tested. The one thing now certain is that thousands of acres of what have been good grazing lands are now absolutely worthless for pasturage. The prairie grasses do not recuperate until at least the second year, when they have been grazed or cut close. This fact, of itself, is enough to make cowmen consider the matter carefully, before adding cattle to what may already be an over-stocked range.
articles.summary: Editorial warning that Bad Lands ranges are near capacity, with some 40,000 more head arriving this year, and urging a halt until spring.

articles.text: Earthquake shocks were felt Thursday evening in South Carolina, West Virginia, Iowo Wisconsin, Maryland and Alabama. Much damage was done and as telegraphic communication has been cut off from Charleston, South Carolina, it is feared that that city is destroyed.
articles.summary: Earthquake shocks felt in several states; Charleston, S.C., cut off and feared destroyed.

articles.text: The cases growing out of the citizens of Billings county refusing to pay taxes to Stark county came up last week in Mandan. In the case of the N. P. Ref. Car Co., the preliminary injunction was sustained by Judge Francis and all the cases will come up at the next term of court.

articles.text: The latest candidate for journalistic honors is the Montana Democrat published at Miles City. The editors are Putman and Martin, the former well-known under his nomme de plume of "Slade." The Democrat is a tri-weekly and will at all times "strive to be worthy of the confidence of the entire people." We wish it success.
articles.summary: Notice of the new tri-weekly Montana Democrat at Miles City, edited by Putman and Martin.

articles.text: A powder magazine belonging to Laflin & Rand in Chicago, was exploded by lightning last Sunday morning and in all directions for miles an earth-quake-like shock was felt. About 130,000 pounds of dynamite and blasting powder were exploded. One person was killed and five mortally wounded. The loss will be over $75,000 to the powder company. The loss on window glass almost surpasses computation. One pane worth $300 was broken in the Board of Trade building, over seven miles from the scene of the explosion.
articles.summary: Lightning explodes a Laflin & Rand powder magazine in Chicago, killing one.

articles.text: If there is one thing more than another that will benefit laboring men, it is in organization. But the very fact of their being organized, when under bad leaders works them the greatest of all mischiefs. A case in point is the strike of 6,000 shoe-lasters in Brockton, Mass., because a poor, old man with a family to support and who happened not to belong to their order, was given work. Alreadly they have lost about $250,000 in wages on account of the strike. With able, cool-headed leaders, even-handed justice will always be meted out to laboring men. The penitentiary for life is too mild a punishment for the man or set of men who ordered this strike.
articles.summary: Editorial on labor organization, condemning the leaders of a Brockton, Mass., shoe-lasters' strike.

articles.text: The round-up of the river outfits closed this morning at the mouth of Davis creek. About twelve cars of beeves were gathered, which will be shipped from Dickinson next Tuesday. The cattle are only in fair condition. Provided they strike a good market there, they will be sold in St. Paul. The Maltese Cross and Elkhorn outfits will have five cars; the Neimmela ranch, two; W. N. Thompson & Co., two and the KC ranch, one. The R quarter-circle outfit will ship two cars from Medora. Messrs. Ferris, Lang, Dantz and Hunt will accompany the cattle to market.

articles.headline: Anderson's Dummy.
articles.text: Chris. Anderson, a northside stockman living on Sunday creek, recently tried a plan of breaking a broncho by tying a dummy on its back. The dummy was made of an old suit of clothes stuffed with straw and somewhat resembled a man. This dummy was tied firmly on the saddle so it could not fall off and the broncho was saddled and turned loose. After some vigorous bucking which [jerked?] off the dummy's head the broncho broke down the corral and ran into a bunch of horses, nearly stampeding them out of the country. While rushing madly along with the limber, flopping, helpless rider on its back, the broncho came in sight of a cowboy returning from recent interviews with Miles City whiskey. Probably the c. b's. vision was none of the clearest then, so thinking to relieve a fellow creature in distress, he jabbed spurs into his horse and flew in pursuit. After a hard and exciting chase he ran up close enough to make a throw with his lariat, and succeeded in missing the horse but caught and stripped off saddle and dummy. Imagine first his horror at finding on the end of his rope a headless man, and a moment after that his relief on learning that it was only Anderson's dummy.—[Montana Democrat.
articles.summary: Reprinted Montana Democrat tale of Chris. Anderson's broncho-breaking dummy near Miles City and a cowboy who roped it.

articles.text: The first herd of cattle known on the continent of America was brought by Columbus on his second voyage. From these, and from other small herds brought by later Spanish navigators, the wild cattle of South America descended. In 1553 the Portugese took cattle and hogs to Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. The Canadian cattle were introduced in 1608. In 1620 Virginia had 500 head of cattle. The most stringent laws were passed prohibiting the killing of any domestic animal. In New England cattle were introduced in 1624. It is said that for a time, price was regulated by color, a red calf being cheaper than a black one because it was more likely to be mistaken by the wolves for a deer and killed.—[Chicago Stock-News.
articles.summary: Reprinted Chicago Stock-News note on the early history of cattle in the Americas.

articles.headline: Better Stock Cars.
articles.text:
This issue of the Record contains a letter from Walter C. Weedon, of Kansas City to the Albuquerque Journal, giving an account of a recent shipment of Arizona cattle in the Burton stock cars, which will be read with interest by stockmen generally. It is really surprising that in such an era of progress the stock car of forty years ago is now in general use, this too, in the face of the fact that they have never been anything but cruel contrivances, which served no other or better purpose than to merely hold stock on the track until the train reached its destination. The railroads have discouraged any innovation on the old method, mainly, of course, on account of the large amount of money already invested in the old-time style of cars, and for the further reason that railroad companies, as a rule, are very slow to adopt any invention which adds anything to their expense account. We believe, however, that the death knell of the old stock car has been sounded at last, and that better facilities must and will be furnished to shippers of live stock. Where competing lines are striving to obtain live stock shipments, instead of monkeying with the tariff and rebate system, improved cars will be offered to the shipper. This will compel other lines to do likewise, and when once the revolution begins it will spread like a prairie fire and improved cars will be the rule.

The Burton car is an undoubted success and is practically a live stock sleeping and dining car. The only reason why it is not generally adopted at sight is the great cost of its construction; but when the railroads generally signify their willingness to take a step forward in the matter, Yankee ingenuity will provide something satisfactory to both the shipper and the railroads, which can be built for a sum not greater than the purpose justifies. The killed and maimed cattle together with the shrinkage directly chargeable to the poorly-fashioned stock cars, have reduced the profits of the range cattlemen millions of dollars, and now that the time has arrived when intelligence and a care for the details must be observed in the range cattle business, the question of better shipping facilities is one that demands careful attention, and there can be no doubt of success if there is unity of action among the cowmen.

The sheepmen have steadily clamored for double-decked cars, and although the railroad companies positively set themselves against the request, the sheep growers were not discouraged, but kept up the fight. They enlisted the stock yard and commission men under their banner, notably Colonel R. D. Hunter, of St. Louis, and their labors have been crowned with success. The Missouri Pacific system and Texas roads have begun the construction of double-deck cars and they will be used by all roads transporting sheep. A like victory awaits the cattlemen if they work for it.—[Colorado L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Reprinted Colorado Live Stock Record article urging better stock cars such as the Burton car.

articles.text: One of Fred Willard's horses made things lively in Dan. McKenzie's blacksmith shop yesterday. It was being tied down, when it broke loose and began scattering things in a way to make a cyclone turn green with envy. It finally broke out of the shop and then bolted through the heavy gate on the Co's. corral, in which it was caught.

articles.text: The last heard of Bob. Thompson, he had stolen four of the best of the 13 horses and gone to parts unknown. This was last Thursday morning. There is scarcely one chance in a thousand of his getting away and when caught he will be sentenced to a long term. Besides the Medora charges of shooting in the public highway, resisting officers, threatening to kill and horse-stealing, there is a charge of murder against him from Strong City, Kansas.
articles.summary: Bob. Thompson stole four horses and fled; he faces Medora charges and a murder charge from Strong City, Kansas.

articles.headline: Weather Review for July.
articles.text:
For the month of July, A. D., 1886, kept at Medora, Billings Co., Dakota, by T. Martin. Latitude; north, 46 degrees, 54 minutes and 45 seconds. Longitude; west, 102 degrees, 29 minutes and 12 seconds.

If there is any place this side of the one Ingersoll says does not exist, that can show a hotter record for one month, it has yet to be heard from.

The month came in dry and warm, with only one and one-tenth inches of rain for the last twenty days, with temperature ranging from eighty-eight to one hundred and ten in the shade.

Following is the mean temperature at six o'clock a. m., twelve m. and six p. m. for both sun and shade, for the thirty-one days of July.

At 6 a. m., in shade, 83 11-100 degrees
" " sun, 87 13-100 "
At 12 m., in shade, 101 30-100 "
" " sun, 110 6-100 "
At 6 p. m., in shade, 92 30-100 "
" " sun, 102 6-100 "
H'g'st temp. in shade at 6 a. m. 98 "
" " " 12 m., 122 "
" " " 6 p. m., 114 "
L'w'st temp. at 6 a. m., in shade, 70 "
" " 12 m. " 66 "
" " 6 p. m. " 70 "

On the 29th., the highest temperature in the sun was 74 degrees. The lowest on the same day was 70 degrees, with a clear sky all day.

During the month, we had twenty-six and one-third clear days, one and one-third fair days and three and one-third cloudy days.

The wind was: N. W., two-thirds of one day; North, two and two-thirds; N. E., six and one-third; East, five; S. E., five and two-thirds; South, five and one-third; S. W., one and one-third; West, three and two-thirds.

During the month we have had one and 13-100 inches of rain-fall.

On the evening of the 28th., there was a brilliant display of northern lights which lasted about fifty minutes. There were also during the month a great number of meteors, mostly in the southern hemisphere and some of them quite large. The number far exceeded any record I have ever seen published.

The warmest day during the month was the 10th. Following is the record of the twelve hours from 6 a. m. to 6 p. m.:

Six o'clock, shade 94, sun 95; 7 o'clock, shade 98, sun 104; 8 o'clock, shade 100, sun 108; 9 o'clock, shade 102, sun 110; 10 o'clock, shade 106, sun 118; 11 o'clock, shade 118, sun 128; 12 o'clock, shade 120, sun 134; 1 o'clock, shade 122, sun 136; 2 o'clock, shade 116, sun 136; 2:20 o'clock, shade 112, sun 134; 4 o'clock, shade 96, sun 108; 5 o'clock, shade 86, sun 92; 6 o'clock, shade 70, sun 76.

You will see there is a variation of 6[0?] degrees in five hours, and at 9:30 p. m. the temperature was 56 degrees.

During the month, the highest temperature in the sun at 6 a. m., was 100 degrees, at noon, 136 degrees and at 6 p. m. 114 degrees.

The heated term still continues up t[o?] this date, August 28, with temperatu[re?] ranging from 80 to 132 degrees in th[e?] sun and 70 to 118 in the shade.

During this heated term, there ha[s?] been no sunstroke or sickness of an[y?] kind. There were several accidents a[nd?] one death by lightning.

T. MARTIN.
articles.summary: T. Martin's weather review for July 1886 at Medora: extreme heat (122 in shade on the 10th), little rain, northern lights on the 28th; heat continuing to August 28.
